Language.comment: A language is a set of strings over an alphabet.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.

Language.description: A language is defined as a collection of strings formed from a given alphabet.

Language.zero_def.description: The zero element of a language corresponds to the empty set.

Language.one_def.description: The one element of a language is represented by the set containing only the empty string.

Language.add_def.code: Language.add_def.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l m : Language α) : l + m = l ∪ m
Language.add_def.description: The addition operation for languages is defined as the union of two languages.

Language.mul_def.code: Language.mul_def.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l m : Language α) : l * m = image2 (fun x x_1 => x ++ x_1) l m

explanatories.Set.image2: The image of a binary function, when applied to two sets, is defined as the resulting set of values obtained by applying the function to all pairs of elements from the sets.

Language.mul_def.description: The multiplication operation for languages is defined as the set of all combinations of concatenating strings from two languages.

Language.kstar_def.code: Language.kstar_def.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : l∗ = {x | ∃ L, x = L.join ∧ ∀ y ∈ L, y ∈ l}

explanatories.List.join: This definition describes a function that merges multiple lists into a single list by concatenating their elements.

Language.kstar_def.description: The Kleene star of a language consists of all strings that can be formed by concatenating zero or more strings from that language.

Language.not_mem_zero.code: Language.not_mem_zero.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (x : List α) : x ∉ 0
Language.not_mem_zero.description: No string can belong to the empty set.

Language.mem_one.code: Language.mem_one.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (x : List α) : x ∈ 1 ↔ x = []
Language.mem_one.description: A list belongs to the singleton language if and only if it is the empty list.

Language.nil_mem_one.description: The empty list is an element of the singleton language.

Language.mem_add.code: Language.mem_add.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l m : Language α) (x : List α) : x ∈ l + m ↔ x ∈ l ∨ x ∈ m
Language.mem_add.description: A string belongs to the union of two languages if and only if it belongs to at least one of the individual languages.

Language.mem_mul.code: Language.mem_mul.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l m : Language α} {x : List α} : x ∈ l * m ↔ ∃ a ∈ l, ∃ b ∈ m, a ++ b = x
Language.mem_mul.description: A string belongs to the product of two languages if and only if it can be formed by concatenating a string from each of the individual languages.

Language.append_mem_mul.code: Language.append_mem_mul.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l m : Language α} {a b : List α} : a ∈ l → b ∈ m → a ++ b ∈ l * m
Language.append_mem_mul.description: The concatenation of two strings from two languages is an element of the product of those languages.

Language.mem_kstar.code: Language.mem_kstar.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l : Language α} {x : List α} : x ∈ l∗ ↔ ∃ L, x = L.join ∧ ∀ y ∈ L, y ∈ l

explanatories.List.join: This definition describes a function that merges multiple lists into a single list by concatenating their elements.

Language.mem_kstar.description: A string belongs to the Kleene star of a language if and only if it can be expressed as the concatenation of some list of strings from that language.

Language.join_mem_kstar.code: Language.join_mem_kstar.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l : Language α} {L : List (List α)} (h : ∀ y ∈ L, y ∈ l) : L.join ∈ l∗

explanatories.List.join: This definition describes a function that merges multiple lists into a single list by concatenating their elements.

Language.join_mem_kstar.description: If every string in a list belongs to a language, then the concatenation of all those strings is also included in the Kleene star of that language.

Language.nil_mem_kstar.code: Language.nil_mem_kstar.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : [] ∈ l∗
Language.nil_mem_kstar.description: The empty string belongs to the Kleene star of any language.

Language.add_self.code: Language.add_self.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : l + l = l
Language.add_self.description: The union of a language with itself is equal to the original language.

Language.map.code: Language.map.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β) : Language α →+* Language β
Language.map.comment: Maps the alphabet of a language.

explanatories.Set.singleton: This defines the operation for creating a singleton set that contains only a specific element.
explanatories.Singleton.singleton: A singleton is a collection that contains exactly one element.
explanatories.Union.union: The union of two elements is defined as the combination of both elements into a single entity.
explanatories.Set.image: This defines the image of a set under a function, producing a new set consisting of all values that result from applying the function to elements of the original set.
explanatories.List.map: This definition describes a function that transforms each element of a list by applying a specified function to it, producing a new list of the transformed elements.
explanatories.Set.image_singleton: The image of a singleton set under a function is the singleton set containing the image of the sole element in the original set.
explanatories.Set.image_image2_distrib: The image of a function transformed by another function, when applied to the image of a binary function over two sets, is equal to the image of a corresponding transformed binary function applied to the images of the sets.
explanatories.List.map_append: This theorem asserts that applying a function to the concatenation of two lists is equivalent to concatenating the results of applying the function to each list separately.
explanatories.Set.image_empty: The image of an empty set under any function is also an empty set.
explanatories.Set.image_union: The image of the union of two sets under a function is equal to the union of the images of each set under that function.

Language.map.fullDefinition: def map (f : α → β) : Language α →+* Language β where   toFun := image (List.map f)   map_zero' := image_empty _   map_one' := image_singleton   map_add' := image_union _   map_mul' _ _ := image_image2_distrib <| map_append _
Language.map.description: The mapping function transforms a language defined over one alphabet into a language defined over another alphabet by applying a function to its elements.

Language.map_id.code: Language.map_id.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : (map id) l = l

explanatories.List.map: This definition describes a function that transforms each element of a list by applying a specified function to it, producing a new list of the transformed elements.

Language.map_id.description: Mapping the identity function on a language results in the same language.

explanatories.List.map: This definition describes a function that transforms each element of a list by applying a specified function to it, producing a new list of the transformed elements.

Language.map_map.description: Mapping two functions consecutively over a language is equivalent to mapping their composed function over that same language.

Language.kstar_def_nonempty.code: Language.kstar_def_nonempty.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : l∗ = {x | ∃ S, x = S.join ∧ ∀ y ∈ S, y ∈ l ∧ y ≠ []}

explanatories.List.join: This definition describes a function that merges multiple lists into a single list by concatenating their elements.

Language.kstar_def_nonempty.description: The Kleene star of a language consists of all non-empty strings that can be formed by concatenating a finite number of strings from that language.

Language.le_iff.code: Language.le_iff.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l m : Language α) : l ≤ m ↔ l + m = m
Language.le_iff.description: One language is a subset of another if and only if their sum is equal to the larger language.

Language.le_mul_congr.code: Language.le_mul_congr.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l₁ l₂ m₁ m₂ : Language α} : l₁ ≤ m₁ → l₂ ≤ m₂ → l₁ * l₂ ≤ m₁ * m₂
Language.le_mul_congr.description: If two languages are each less than or equal to two other languages, then their product is also less than or equal to the product of those two other languages.

Language.le_add_congr.code: Language.le_add_congr.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {l₁ l₂ m₁ m₂ : Language α} : l₁ ≤ m₁ → l₂ ≤ m₂ → l₁ + l₂ ≤ m₁ + m₂
Language.le_add_congr.description: If one language is a subset of another and a second language is a subset of a third, then the union of the first two languages is a subset of the union of the last two languages.

Language.mem_iSup.code: Language.mem_iSup.{v, u_1} {α : Type u_1} {ι : Sort v} {l : ι → Language α} {x : List α} : x ∈ ⨆ i, l i ↔ ∃ i, x ∈ l i
Language.mem_iSup.description: A string belongs to the supremum of a collection of languages if and only if it belongs to at least one of the languages in that collection.

Language.iSup_mul.code:
Language.iSup_mul.{v, u_1} {α : Type u_1} {ι : Sort v} (l : ι → Language α) (m : Language α) :
  (⨆ i, l i) * m = ⨆ i, l i * m
Language.iSup_mul.description: The supremum of a family of languages multiplied by another language is equal to the supremum of the products of each language in the family with that language.

Language.mul_iSup.code:
Language.mul_iSup.{v, u_1} {α : Type u_1} {ι : Sort v} (l : ι → Language α) (m : Language α) :
  m * ⨆ i, l i = ⨆ i, m * l i
Language.mul_iSup.description: The product of a language and the supremum of a family of languages is equal to the supremum of the products of that language with each individual language in the family.

Language.iSup_add.code:
Language.iSup_add.{v, u_1} {α : Type u_1} {ι : Sort v} [Nonempty ι] (l : ι → Language α) (m : Language α) :
  (⨆ i, l i) + m = ⨆ i, l i + m
Language.iSup_add.description: The supremum of a family of languages added to another language is equal to the supremum of that family added to the other language.

Language.add_iSup.code:
Language.add_iSup.{v, u_1} {α : Type u_1} {ι : Sort v} [Nonempty ι] (l : ι → Language α) (m : Language α) :
  m + ⨆ i, l i = ⨆ i, m + l i
Language.add_iSup.description: The sum of a language and the supremum of a family of languages is equal to the supremum of the sums of the individual languages from that family with the given language.

Language.mem_pow.code:

explanatories.List.length: This defines a function that computes the number of elements in a list, where the length of an empty list is zero and the length of a non-empty list is one plus the length of its tail.

Language.mem_pow.description: A string belongs to the n-th power of a language if and only if it can be represented as the concatenation of n strings from that language.

Language.kstar_eq_iSup_pow.code: Language.kstar_eq_iSup_pow.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : l∗ = ⨆ i, l ^ i

Language.map_kstar.code: Language.map_kstar.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β) (l : Language α) : (map f) l∗ = ((map f) l)∗

Language.map_kstar.description: The Kleene star of the language transformed by a function is the same as the transformation of the Kleene star of the original language by that function.

Language.mul_self_kstar_comm.code: Language.mul_self_kstar_comm.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : l∗ * l = l * l∗
Language.mul_self_kstar_comm.description: The product of the Kleene star of a language with that language is commutative.

Language.one_add_self_mul_kstar_eq_kstar.code: Language.one_add_self_mul_kstar_eq_kstar.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : 1 + l * l∗ = l∗
Language.one_add_self_mul_kstar_eq_kstar.description: The sum of the singleton language and the product of a language with its Kleene star is equal to the Kleene star of that language.

Language.one_add_kstar_mul_self_eq_kstar.code: Language.one_add_kstar_mul_self_eq_kstar.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (l : Language α) : 1 + l∗ * l = l∗
Language.one_add_kstar_mul_self_eq_kstar.description: The Kleene star of a language is equal to the sum of the language's Kleene star and the language itself when added to the unit language.

explanatories.Union.union: The union of two elements is defined as the combination of both elements into a single entity.
explanatories.rfl: An element is equal to itself, with an implicit argument allowing for broader applications of this concept.
explanatories.Language.zero_def: The zero element of a language corresponds to the empty set.
explanatories.Language.one_def: The one element of a language is represented by the set containing only the empty string.
explanatories.Language.add_def: The addition operation for languages is defined as the union of two languages.
explanatories.Language.mul_def: The multiplication operation for languages is defined as the set of all combinations of concatenating strings from two languages.
explanatories.Iff.rfl: Any proposition is equivalent to itself.

explanatories.Set.union_empty: The union of a set with the empty set is equal to the original set.

explanatories.Set.image2_union_left: The image of a binary function applied to the union of two sets with a third set is equal to the union of the images obtained by applying the function to each of the individual sets with the third set.

explanatories.Nat.cast: This defines a canonical function that converts natural numbers into another type while preserving the structure of addition and multiplication.
explanatories.mul_assoc: This theorem asserts that multiplication in a semigroup is associative, meaning the product of three elements is the same regardless of how they are grouped.

Language.instSemiring.fullDefinition: instance instSemiring : Semiring (Language α) where   add := (· + ·)   add_assoc := union_assoc   zero := 0   zero_add := empty_union   add_zero := union_empty   add_comm := union_comm   mul := (· * ·)   mul_assoc _ _ _ := image2_assoc append_assoc   zero_mul _ := image2_empty_left   mul_zero _ := image2_empty_right   one := 1   one_mul l := by simp [mul_def, one_def]   mul_one l := by simp [mul_def, one_def]   natCast n := if n = 0 then 0 else 1   natCast_zero := rfl   natCast_succ n := by cases n <;> simp [Nat.cast, add_def, zero_def]   left_distrib _ _ _ := image2_union_right   right_distrib _ _ _ := image2_union_left   nsmul := nsmulRec
Language.instSemiring.description: A semiring structure is defined for languages, which are sets of strings over a given alphabet.

Turing.ListBlank.bind.fullDefinition: def ListBlank.bind {Γ Γ'} [Inhabited Γ] [Inhabited Γ'] (l : ListBlank Γ) (f : Γ → List Γ')     (hf : ∃ n, f default = List.replicate n default) : ListBlank Γ' := by   apply l.liftOn (fun l ↦ ListBlank.mk (List.bind l f))   rintro l _ ⟨i, rfl⟩; cases' hf with n e; refine Quotient.sound' (Or.inl ⟨i * n, ?_⟩)   rw [List.append_bind, mul_comm]; congr   induction' i with i IH   · rfl   simp only [IH, e, List.replicate_add, Nat.mul_succ, add_comm, List.replicate_succ, List.cons_bind]

Turing.Respects.comment:
Given a relation `tr : σ₁ → σ₂ → Prop` between state spaces, and state transition functions
`f₁ : σ₁ → Option σ₁` and `f₂ : σ₂ → Option σ₂`, `Respects f₁ f₂ tr` means that if `tr a₁ a₂` holds
initially and `f₁` takes a step to `a₂` then `f₂` will take one or more steps before reaching a
state `b₂` satisfying `tr a₂ b₂`, and if `f₁ a₁` terminates then `f₂ a₂` also terminates.
Such a relation `tr` is also known as a refinement.

Turing.TM0.Machine.comment:
A Post-Turing machine with symbol type `Γ` and label type `Λ`
is a function which, given the current state `q : Λ` and
the tape head `a : Γ`, either halts (returns `none`) or returns
a new state `q' : Λ` and a `Stmt` describing what to do,
either a move left or right, or a write command.

Both `Λ` and `Γ` are required to be inhabited; the default value
for `Γ` is the "blank" tape value, and the default value of `Λ` is
the initial state.

Turing.TM0.Supports.code: Turing.TM0.Supports.{u_1, u_2} {Γ : Type u_1} {Λ : Type u_2} [Inhabited Λ] (M : Machine₀) (S : Set Λ) : Prop
Turing.TM0.Supports.comment:
The raw definition of a Turing machine does not require that
`Γ` and `Λ` are finite, and in practice we will be interested
in the infinite `Λ` case. We recover instead a notion of
"effectively finite" Turing machines, which only make use of a
finite subset of their states. We say that a set `S ⊆ Λ`
supports a Turing machine `M` if `S` is closed under the
transition function and contains the initial state.

Turing.TM1to0.Λ'.code:
Turing.TM1to0.Λ'.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {Γ : Type u_1} {Λ : Type u_2} {σ : Type u_3} (M : Λ → Stmt₁) :
  Type (max (max (max u_3 u_2) u_1) u_3)
Turing.TM1to0.Λ'.comment:
The base machine state space is a pair of an `Option Stmt₁` representing the current program
to be executed, or `none` for the halt state, and a `σ` which is the local state (stored in the TM,
not the tape). Because there are an infinite number of programs, this state space is infinite, but
for a finitely supported TM1 machine and a finite type `σ`, only finitely many of these states are
reachable.

Turing.TM1to0.trAux.code:
Turing.TM1to0.trAux.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {Γ : Type u_1} {Λ : Type u_2} {σ : Type u_3} (M : Λ → Stmt₁) (s : Γ) :
  Stmt₁ → σ → Λ'₁₀ × Stmt₀
Turing.TM1to0.trAux.comment:
The core TM1 → TM0 translation function. Here `s` is the current value on the tape, and the
`Stmt₁` is the TM1 statement to translate, with local state `v : σ`. We evaluate all regular
instructions recursively until we reach either a `move` or `write` command, or a `goto`; in the
latter case we emit a dummy `write s` step and transition to the new target location.

Turing.TM1to0.trAux.fullDefinition: def trAux (s : Γ) : Stmt₁ → σ → Λ'₁₀ × Stmt₀   | TM1.Stmt.move d q, v => ((some q, v), move d)   | TM1.Stmt.write a q, v => ((some q, v), write (a s v))   | TM1.Stmt.load a q, v => trAux s q (a s v)   | TM1.Stmt.branch p q₁ q₂, v => cond (p s v) (trAux s q₁ v) (trAux s q₂ v)   | TM1.Stmt.goto l, v => ((some (M (l s v)), v), write s)   | TM1.Stmt.halt, v => ((none, v), write s)

S   | pop k f q, v, S => stepAux q (f v (S k).head?) (update S k (S k).tail)   | load a q, v, S => stepAux q (a v) S   | branch f q₁ q₂, v, S => cond (f v) (stepAux q₁ v S) (stepAux q₂ v S)   | goto f, v, S => ⟨some (f v), v, S⟩   | halt, v, S => ⟨none, v, S⟩

Turing.TM2to1.stmtStRec.comment:
We have partitioned the TM2 statements into "stack actions", which require going to the end
of the stack, and all other actions, which do not. This is a modified recursor which lumps the
stack actions into one.

Turing.TM2to1.stmtStRec.fullDefinition: def stmtStRec.{l} {C : Stmt₂ → Sort l} (H₁ : ∀ (k) (s : StAct₂ k) (q) (_ : C q), C (stRun s q))     (H₂ : ∀ (a q) (_ : C q), C (TM2.Stmt.load a q))     (H₃ : ∀ (p q₁ q₂) (_ : C q₁) (_ : C q₂), C (TM2.Stmt.branch p q₁ q₂))     (H₄ : ∀ l, C (TM2.Stmt.goto l)) (H₅ : C TM2.Stmt.halt) : ∀ n, C n   | TM2.Stmt.push _ f q => H₁ _ (push f) _ (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q)   | TM2.Stmt.peek _ f q => H₁ _ (peek f) _ (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q)   | TM2.Stmt.pop _ f q => H₁ _ (pop f) _ (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q)   | TM2.Stmt.load _ q => H₂ _ _ (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q)   | TM2.Stmt.branch _ q₁ q₂ => H₃ _ _ _ (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q₁) (stmtStRec H₁ H₂ H₃ H₄ H₅ q₂)   | TM2.Stmt.goto _ => H₄ _   | TM2.Stmt.halt => H₅

Turing.TM2to1.tr.eq_1.code:
Turing.TM2to1.tr.eq_1.{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4} {K : Type u_1} [DecidableEq K] {Γ : K → Type u_2} {Λ : Type u_3}
  {σ : Type u_4} (M : Λ → Stmt₂) :
  ∀ (x : Λ'),
    tr M x =
      match x with
      | normal q => trNormal (M q)
      | go k s q =>
        branch (fun a x => (a.2 k).isNone) (trStAct (goto fun x x => ret q) s)
          (move Dir.right (goto fun x x => go k s q))
      | ret q => branch (fun a x => a.1) (trNormal q) (move Dir.left (goto fun x x => ret q))

Turing.TM2to1.tr_respects_aux.{u_1, u_2, u_3, u_4} {K : Type u_1} [DecidableEq K] {Γ : K → Type u_2} {Λ : Type u_3}
  {σ : Type u_4} (M : Λ → Stmt₂) {q : Stmt₂} {v : σ} {T : ListBlank ((i : K) → Option (Γ i))} {k : K}
  {S : (k : K) → List (Γ k)} (hT : ∀ (k : K), ListBlank.map (proj k) T = ListBlank.mk (List.map some (S k)).reverse)
  (o : StAct k)
  (IH :
    ∀ {v : σ} {S : (k : K) → List (Γ k)} {T : ListBlank ((k : K) → Option (Γ k))},
      (∀ (k : K), ListBlank.map (proj k) T = ListBlank.mk (List.map some (S k)).reverse) →
        ∃ b,
          TrCfg (TM2.stepAux q v S) b ∧
            Reaches (TM1.step (tr M)) (TM1.stepAux (trNormal q) v (Tape.mk' ∅ (addBottom T))) b) :
  ∃ b,
    TrCfg (TM2.stepAux (stRun o q) v S) b ∧
      Reaches (TM1.step (tr M)) (TM1.stepAux (trNormal (stRun o q)) v (Tape.mk' ∅ (addBottom T))) b

Primcodable.list.fullDefinition: instance list : Primcodable (List α) :=   ⟨letI H := @Primcodable.prim (List ℕ) _     have : Primrec₂ fun (a : α) (o : Option (List ℕ)) => o.map (List.cons (encode a)) :=       option_map snd <| (list_cons' H).comp ((@Primrec.encode α _).comp (fst.comp fst)) snd     have :       Primrec fun n =>         (ofNat (List ℕ) n).reverse.foldl           (fun o m => (@decode α _ m).bind fun a => o.map (List.cons (encode a))) (some []) :=       list_foldl' H ((list_reverse' H).comp (.ofNat (List ℕ))) (const (some []))         (Primrec.comp₂ (bind_decode_iff.2 <| .swap this) Primrec₂.right)     nat_iff.1 <|       (encode_iff.2 this).of_eq fun n => by         rw [List.foldl_reverse]         apply Nat.case_strong_induction_on n; · simp         intro n IH; simp         cases' @decode α _ n.unpair.1 with a; · rfl         simp only [decode_eq_ofNat, Option.some.injEq, Option.some_bind, Option.map_some']         suffices ∀ (o : Option (List ℕ)) (p), encode o = encode p →             encode (Option.map (List.cons (encode a)) o) = encode (Option.map (List.cons a) p) from           this _ _ (IH _ (Nat.unpair_right_le n))         intro o p IH         cases o <;> cases p         · rfl         · injection IH         · injection IH         · exact congr_arg (fun k => (Nat.pair (encode a) k).succ.succ) (Nat.succ.inj IH)⟩

Nat.rfindX.fullDefinition: def rfindX : { n // true ∈ p n ∧ ∀ m < n, false ∈ p m } :=   suffices ∀ k, (∀ n < k, false ∈ p n) → { n // true ∈ p n ∧ ∀ m < n, false ∈ p m } from     this 0 fun n => (Nat.not_lt_zero _).elim   @WellFounded.fix _ _ (lbp p) (wf_lbp p H)     (by       intro m IH al       have pm : (p m).Dom := by         rcases H with ⟨n, h₁, h₂⟩         rcases lt_trichotomy m n with (h₃ | h₃ | h₃)         · exact h₂ _ h₃         · rw [h₃]           exact h₁.fst         · injection mem_unique h₁ (al _ h₃)       cases e : (p m).get pm       · suffices ∀ᵉ k ≤ m, false ∈ p k from IH _ ⟨rfl, this⟩ fun n h => this _ (le_of_lt_succ h)         intro n h         cases' h.lt_or_eq_dec with h h         · exact al _ h         · rw [h]           exact ⟨_, e⟩       · exact ⟨m, ⟨_, e⟩, al⟩)

ack.comment:
The two-argument Ackermann function, defined so that

- `ack 0 n = n + 1`
- `ack (m + 1) 0 = ack m 1`
- `ack (m + 1) (n + 1) = ack m (ack (m + 1) n)`.

This is of interest as both a fast-growing function, and as an example of a recursive function that
isn't primitive recursive.
ack.fullDefinition: def ack : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ   | 0, n => n + 1   | m + 1, 0 => ack m 1   | m + 1, n + 1 => ack m (ack (m + 1) n)
ack.description: The two-argument Ackermann function is a recursive function that grows rapidly and is notable for being non-primitive recursive, defined by specific rules for its computation based on the values of its arguments.

ack.eq_1.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument equal to zero is always one more than the second argument.

ack_zero.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument equal to zero is always one more than the second argument.

ack.eq_2.code: ack.eq_2 (m : ℕ) : ack m.succ 0 = ack m 1
ack.eq_2.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument as the successor of a natural number is equal to the value of the function with that number and one as the second argument.

ack_succ_zero.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function evaluated at the successor of a natural number and zero is equal to the value of the function evaluated at that natural number and one.

ack.eq_3.code: ack.eq_3 (m n : ℕ) : ack m.succ n.succ = ack m (ack (m + 1) n)
ack.eq_3.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument as the successor of a natural number and the second argument as the successor of another natural number is equal to the value of the function with the first argument and the result of applying the Ackermann function to the successor of the first argument and the second argument.

ack_succ_succ.code: ack_succ_succ (m n : ℕ) : ack (m + 1) (n + 1) = ack m (ack (m + 1) n)
ack_succ_succ.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function evaluated at the successor of two natural numbers is equal to the value of the function with the first number and the result of evaluating the function at the successor of the first number with the second number.

ack_one.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument fixed at one is equal to the second argument increased by two.

ack_two.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument equal to two is equal to twice the second argument plus three.

ack_three.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function with the first argument equal to three is equal to two raised to the power of the second argument plus three, minus three.

ack_pos.code: ack_pos (m n : ℕ) : 0 < ack m n
ack_pos.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function is always a positive number for any non-negative integer inputs.

one_lt_ack_succ_left.description: The value of the Ackermann function with the first argument as one more than a natural number is always greater than one for any natural number as the second argument.

one_lt_ack_succ_right.description: The value of the two-argument Ackermann function evaluated at a natural number and the successor of another natural number is always greater than one.

explanatories.StrictMono: A function is considered strictly monotone if it maintains the order relationship such that whenever one input is strictly less than another, the output corresponding to the first input is also strictly less than the output corresponding to the second input.

ack_strictMono_right.description: The two-argument Ackermann function is strictly monotonic when its first argument is held constant and the second argument varies.

explanatories.Monotone: A function is considered monotone if it preserves the order, meaning that if one input is less than or equal to another, then the output will not exceed the corresponding output of the larger input.

ack_mono_right.description: The two-argument Ackermann function is monotonic when its first argument is held constant and the second argument varies.

explanatories.Function.Injective: This definition specifies a property of a function that ensures distinct inputs are mapped to distinct outputs.

ack_injective_right.description: The function defined by the Ackermann formula with a fixed first argument is injective, meaning it produces unique outputs for different inputs.

ack_lt_iff_right.code: ack_lt_iff_right {m n₁ n₂ : ℕ} : ack m n₁ < ack m n₂ ↔ n₁ < n₂
ack_lt_iff_right.description: The inequality of the two-argument Ackermann function evaluated at the same first argument is equivalent to the inequality of the second arguments.

ack_le_iff_right.code: ack_le_iff_right {m n₁ n₂ : ℕ} : ack m n₁ ≤ ack m n₂ ↔ n₁ ≤ n₂
ack_le_iff_right.description: The two-argument Ackermann function with a fixed first argument preserves the order of its second argument, such that the output is less than or equal to the output for a larger second argument if and only if the second arguments themselves are in the same order.

ack_inj_right.code: ack_inj_right {m n₁ n₂ : ℕ} : ack m n₁ = ack m n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂
ack_inj_right.description: The equality of the two-argument Ackermann function evaluated at the same first argument implies the equality of the second arguments.

explanatories.StrictMono: A function is considered strictly monotone if it maintains the order relationship such that whenever one input is strictly less than another, the output corresponding to the first input is also strictly less than the output corresponding to the second input.

ack_mono_left.code: ack_mono_left (n : ℕ) : Monotone fun m => ack m n

Nat.Partrec.Code.ofNatCode.fullDefinition: def ofNatCode : ℕ → Code   | 0 => zero   | 1 => succ   | 2 => left   | 3 => right   | n + 4 =>     let m := n.div2.div2     have hm : m < n + 4 := by       simp only [m, div2_val]       exact         lt_of_le_of_lt (le_trans (Nat.div_le_self _ _) (Nat.div_le_self _ _))           (Nat.succ_le_succ (Nat.le_add_right _ _))     have _m1 : m.unpair.1 < n + 4 := lt_of_le_of_lt m.unpair_left_le hm     have _m2 : m.unpair.2 < n + 4 := lt_of_le_of_lt m.unpair_right_le hm     match n.bodd, n.div2.bodd with     | false, false => pair (ofNatCode m.unpair.1) (ofNatCode m.unpair.2)     | false, true  => comp (ofNatCode m.unpair.1) (ofNatCode m.unpair.2)     | true , false => prec (ofNatCode m.unpair.1) (ofNatCode m.unpair.2)     | true , true  => rfind' (ofNatCode m)

Nat.Partrec.Code.ofNatCode.eq_5.code:
Nat.Partrec.Code.ofNatCode.eq_5 (n : ℕ) :
  ofNatCode n.succ.succ.succ.succ =
    match n.bodd, n.div2.bodd with
    | false, false => (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).1).pair (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).2)
    | false, true => (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).1).comp (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).2)
    | true, false => (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).1).prec (ofNatCode (unpair n.div2.div2).2)
    | true, true => (ofNatCode n.div2.div2).rfind'

Nat.Partrec.Code.eval.comment:
The interpretation of a `Nat.Partrec.Code` as a partial function.
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.zero`: The constant zero function.
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.succ`: The successor function.
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.left`: Left unpairing of a pair of ℕ (encoded by `Nat.pair`)
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.right`: Right unpairing of a pair of ℕ (encoded by `Nat.pair`)
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.pair`: Pairs the outputs of argument codes using `Nat.pair`.
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.comp`: Composition of two argument codes.
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.prec`: Primitive recursion. Given an argument of the form `Nat.pair a n`:
  * If `n = 0`, returns `eval cf a`.
  * If `n = succ k`, returns `eval cg (pair a (pair k (eval (prec cf cg) (pair a k))))`
* `Nat.Partrec.Code.rfind'`: Minimization. For `f` an argument of the form `Nat.pair a m`,
  `rfind' f m` returns the least `a` such that `f a m = 0`, if one exists and `f b m` terminates
  for `b < a`

Nat.Partrec.Code.eval.fullDefinition: def eval : Code → ℕ →. ℕ   | zero => pure 0   | succ => Nat.succ   | left => ↑fun n : ℕ => n.unpair.1   | right => ↑fun n : ℕ => n.unpair.2   | pair cf cg => fun n => Nat.pair <$> eval cf n <*> eval cg n   | comp cf cg => fun n => eval cg n >>= eval cf   | prec cf cg =>     Nat.unpaired fun a n =>       n.rec (eval cf a) fun y IH => do         let i ← IH         eval cg (Nat.pair a (Nat.pair y i))   | rfind' cf =>     Nat.unpaired fun a m =>       (Nat.rfind fun n => (fun m => m = 0) <$> eval cf (Nat.pair a (n + m))).map (· + m)

Nat.Partrec.Code.evaln.comment:
A modified evaluation for the code which returns an `Option ℕ` instead of a `Part ℕ`. To avoid
undecidability, `evaln` takes a parameter `k` and fails if it encounters a number ≥ k in the course
of its execution. Other than this, the semantics are the same as in `Nat.Partrec.Code.eval`.

Nat.Partrec.Code.evaln.fullDefinition: def evaln : ℕ → Code → ℕ → Option ℕ   | 0, _ => fun _ => Option.none   | k + 1, zero => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     return 0   | k + 1, succ => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     return (Nat.succ n)   | k + 1, left => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     return n.unpair.1   | k + 1, right => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     pure n.unpair.2   | k + 1, pair cf cg => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     Nat.pair <$> evaln (k + 1) cf n <*> evaln (k + 1) cg n   | k + 1, comp cf cg => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     let x ← evaln (k + 1) cg n     evaln (k + 1) cf x   | k + 1, prec cf cg => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     n.unpaired fun a n =>       n.casesOn (evaln (k + 1) cf a) fun y => do         let i ← evaln k (prec cf cg) (Nat.pair a y)         evaln (k + 1) cg (Nat.pair a (Nat.pair y i))   | k + 1, rfind' cf => fun n => do     guard (n ≤ k)     n.unpaired fun a m => do       let x ← evaln (k + 1) cf (Nat.pair a m)       if x = 0 then         pure m       else         evaln k (rfind' cf) (Nat.pair a (m + 1))

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval.code: Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval : Code → List ℕ →. List ℕ
Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval.comment:
The semantics of the `Code` primitives, as partial functions `List ℕ →. List ℕ`. By convention
we functions that return a single result return a singleton `[n]`, or in some cases `n :: v` where
`v` will be ignored by a subsequent function.

* `zero'` appends a `0` to the input. That is, `zero' v = 0 :: v`.
* `succ` returns the successor of the head of the input, defaulting to zero if there is no head:
  * `succ [] = [1]`
  * `succ (n :: v) = [n + 1]`
* `tail` returns the tail of the input
  * `tail [] = []`
  * `tail (n :: v) = v`
* `cons f fs` calls `f` and `fs` on the input and conses the results:
  * `cons f fs v = (f v).head :: fs v`
* `comp f g` calls `f` on the output of `g`:
  * `comp f g v = f (g v)`
* `case f g` cases on the head of the input, calling `f` or `g` depending on whether it is zero or
  a successor (similar to `Nat.casesOn`).
  * `case f g [] = f []`
  * `case f g (0 :: v) = f v`
  * `case f g (n+1 :: v) = g (n :: v)`
* `fix f` calls `f` repeatedly, using the head of the result of `f` to decide whether to call `f`
  again or finish:
  * `fix f v = []` if `f v = []`
  * `fix f v = w` if `f v = 0 :: w`
  * `fix f v = fix f w` if `f v = n+1 :: w` (the exact value of `n` is discarded)

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval.fullDefinition: def Code.eval : Code → List ℕ →. List ℕ   | Code.zero' => fun v => pure (0 :: v)   | Code.succ => fun v => pure [v.headI.succ]   | Code.tail => fun v => pure v.tail   | Code.cons f fs => fun v => do     let n ← Code.eval f v     let ns ← Code.eval fs v     pure (n.headI :: ns)   | Code.comp f g => fun v => g.eval v >>= f.eval   | Code.case f g => fun v => v.headI.rec (f.eval v.tail) fun y _ => g.eval (y::v.tail)   | Code.fix f =>     PFun.fix fun v => (f.eval v).map fun v => if v.headI = 0 then Sum.inl v.tail else Sum.inr v.tail

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.rfind.comment:
`rfind f` performs the function of the `rfind` primitive of partial recursive functions.
`rfind f v` returns the smallest `n` such that `(f (n :: v)).head = 0`.

It is implemented as:

    rfind f v = pred (fix (fun (n::v) => f (n::v) :: n+1 :: v) (0 :: v))

The idea is that the initial state is `0 :: v`, and the `fix` keeps `n :: v` as its internal state;
it calls `f (n :: v)` as the exit test and `n+1 :: v` as the next state. At the end we get
`n+1 :: v` where `n` is the desired output, and `pred (n+1 :: v) = [n]` returns the result.

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.prec.comment:
`prec f g` implements the `prec` (primitive recursion) operation of partial recursive
functions. `prec f g` evaluates as:

* `prec f g [] = [f []]`
* `prec f g (0 :: v) = [f v]`
* `prec f g (n+1 :: v) = [g (n :: prec f g (n :: v) :: v)]`

It is implemented as:

    G (a :: b :: IH :: v) = (b :: a+1 :: b-1 :: g (a :: IH :: v) :: v)
    F (0 :: f_v :: v) = (f_v :: v)
    F (n+1 :: f_v :: v) = (fix G (0 :: n :: f_v :: v)).tail.tail
    prec f g (a :: v) = [(F (a :: f v :: v)).head]

Because `fix` always evaluates its body at least once, we must special case the `0` case to avoid
calling `g` more times than necessary (which could be bad if `g` diverges). If the input is
`0 :: v`, then `F (0 :: f v :: v) = (f v :: v)` so we return `[f v]`. If the input is `n+1 :: v`,
we evaluate the function from the bottom up, with initial state `0 :: n :: f v :: v`. The first
number counts up, providing arguments for the applications to `g`, while the second number counts
down, providing the exit condition (this is the initial `b` in the return value of `G`, which is
stripped by `fix`). After the `fix` is complete, the final state is `n :: 0 :: res :: v` where
`res` is the desired result, and the rest reduces this to `[res]`.

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.exists_code.comp {m n : ℕ} {f : Vector ℕ n →. ℕ} {g : Fin n → Vector ℕ m →. ℕ}
  (hf : ∃ c, ∀ (v : Vector ℕ n), c.eval ↑v = pure <$> f v)
  (hg : ∀ (i : Fin n), ∃ c, ∀ (v : Vector ℕ m), c.eval ↑v = pure <$> g i v) :
  ∃ c, ∀ (v : Vector ℕ m), c.eval ↑v = pure <$> ((Vector.mOfFn fun i => g i v) >>= f)

Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.eval.fullDefinition: def Cont.eval : Cont → List ℕ →. List ℕ   | Cont.halt => pure   | Cont.cons₁ fs as k => fun v => do     let ns ← Code.eval fs as     Cont.eval k (v.headI :: ns)   | Cont.cons₂ ns k => fun v => Cont.eval k (ns.headI :: v)   | Cont.comp f k => fun v => Code.eval f v >>= Cont.eval k   | Cont.fix f k => fun v => if v.headI = 0 then k.eval v.tail else f.fix.eval v.tail >>= k.eval

Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.code: Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal : Code → Cont → List ℕ → Cfg
Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.comment:
Evaluating `c : Code` in a continuation `k : Cont` and input `v : List ℕ`. This goes by
recursion on `c`, building an augmented continuation and a value to pass to it.

* `zero' v = 0 :: v` evaluates immediately, so we return it to the parent continuation
* `succ v = [v.headI.succ]` evaluates immediately, so we return it to the parent continuation
* `tail v = v.tail` evaluates immediately, so we return it to the parent continuation
* `cons f fs v = (f v).headI :: fs v` requires two sub-evaluations, so we evaluate
  `f v` in the continuation `k (_.headI :: fs v)` (called `Cont.cons₁ fs v k`)
* `comp f g v = f (g v)` requires two sub-evaluations, so we evaluate
  `g v` in the continuation `k (f _)` (called `Cont.comp f k`)
* `case f g v = v.head.casesOn (f v.tail) (fun n => g (n :: v.tail))` has the information needed
  to evaluate the case statement, so we do that and transition to either
  `f v` or `g (n :: v.tail)`.
* `fix f v = let v' := f v; if v'.headI = 0 then k v'.tail else fix f v'.tail`
  needs to first evaluate `f v`, so we do that and leave the rest for the continuation (called
  `Cont.fix f k`)

Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.fullDefinition: def stepNormal : Code → Cont → List ℕ → Cfg   | Code.zero' => fun k v => Cfg.ret k (0::v)   | Code.succ => fun k v => Cfg.ret k [v.headI.succ]   | Code.tail => fun k v => Cfg.ret k v.tail   | Code.cons f fs => fun k v => stepNormal f (Cont.cons₁ fs v k) v   | Code.comp f g => fun k v => stepNormal g (Cont.comp f k) v   | Code.case f g => fun k v =>     v.headI.rec (stepNormal f k v.tail) fun y _ => stepNormal g k (y::v.tail)   | Code.fix f => fun k v => stepNormal f (Cont.fix f k) v
Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.description: This definition outlines a process for evaluating a specific code in Turing computations using a continuation and an input list, recursively handling various operations by either returning immediate results or transitioning through continuations for further evaluations.

Turing.ToPartrec.stepRet.comment:
Evaluating a continuation `k : Cont` on input `v : List ℕ`. This is the second part of
evaluation, when we receive results from continuations built by `stepNormal`.

* `Cont.halt v = v`, so we are done and transition to the `Cfg.halt v` state
* `Cont.cons₁ fs as k v = k (v.headI :: fs as)`, so we evaluate `fs as` now with the continuation
  `k (v.headI :: _)` (called `cons₂ v k`).
* `Cont.cons₂ ns k v = k (ns.headI :: v)`, where we now have everything we need to evaluate
  `ns.headI :: v`, so we return it to `k`.
* `Cont.comp f k v = k (f v)`, so we call `f v` with `k` as the continuation.
* `Cont.fix f k v = k (if v.headI = 0 then k v.tail else fix f v.tail)`, where `v` is a value,
  so we evaluate the if statement and either call `k` with `v.tail`, or call `fix f v` with `k` as
  the continuation (which immediately calls `f` with `Cont.fix f k` as the continuation).

Turing.ToPartrec.step.comment:
If we are not done (in `Cfg.halt` state), then we must be still stuck on a continuation, so
this main loop calls `stepRet` with the new continuation. The overall `step` function transitions
from one `Cfg` to another, only halting at the `Cfg.halt` state.

Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.then.comment:
In order to extract a compositional semantics from the sequential execution behavior of
configurations, we observe that continuations have a monoid structure, with `Cont.halt` as the unit
and `Cont.then` as the multiplication. `Cont.then k₁ k₂` runs `k₁` until it halts, and then takes
the result of `k₁` and passes it to `k₂`.

We will not prove it is associative (although it is), but we are instead interested in the
associativity law `k₂ (eval c k₁) = eval c (k₁.then k₂)`. This holds at both the sequential and
compositional levels, and allows us to express running a machine without the ambient continuation
and relate it to the original machine's evaluation steps. In the literature this is usually
where one uses Turing machines embedded inside other Turing machines, but this approach allows us
to avoid changing the ambient type `Cfg` in the middle of the recursion.

Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal_then.code:
Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal_then (c : Code) (k k' : Cont) (v : List ℕ) :
  stepNormal c (k.then k') v = (stepNormal c k v).then k'
Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal_then.comment:
The `stepNormal` function respects the `then k'` homomorphism. Note that this is an exact
equality, not a simulation; the original and embedded machines move in lock-step until the
embedded machine reaches the halt state.

Turing.ToPartrec.Code.Ok.comment:
This is a temporary definition, because we will prove in `code_is_ok` that it always holds.
It asserts that `c` is semantically correct; that is, for any `k` and `v`,
`eval (stepNormal c k v) = eval (Cfg.ret k (Code.eval c v))`, as an equality of partial values
(so one diverges iff the other does).

In particular, we can let `k = Cont.halt`, and then this asserts that `stepNormal c Cont.halt v`
evaluates to `Cfg.halt (Code.eval c v)`.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr.fullDefinition: def tr : Λ' → Stmt'   | Λ'.move p k₁ k₂ q =>     pop' k₁ <|       branch (fun s => s.elim true p) (goto fun _ => q)         (push' k₂ <| goto fun _ => Λ'.move p k₁ k₂ q)   | Λ'.push k f q =>     branch (fun s => (f s).isSome) ((push k fun s => (f s).iget) <| goto fun _ => q)       (goto fun _ => q)   | Λ'.read q => goto q   | Λ'.clear p k q =>     pop' k <| branch (fun s => s.elim true p) (goto fun _ => q) (goto fun _ => Λ'.clear p k q)   | Λ'.copy q =>     pop' rev <|       branch Option.isSome (push' main <| push' stack <| goto fun _ => Λ'.copy q) (goto fun _ => q)   | Λ'.succ q =>     pop' main <|       branch (fun s => s = some Γ'.bit1) ((push rev fun _ => Γ'.bit0) <| goto fun _ => Λ'.succ q) <|         branch (fun s => s = some Γ'.cons)           ((push main fun _ => Γ'.cons) <| (push main fun _ => Γ'.bit1) <| goto fun _ => unrev q)           ((push main fun _ => Γ'.bit1) <| goto fun _ => unrev q)   | Λ'.pred q₁ q₂ =>     pop' main <|       branch (fun s => s = some Γ'.bit0)           ((push rev fun _ => Γ'.bit1) <| goto fun _ => Λ'.pred q₁ q₂) <|         branch (fun s => natEnd s.iget) (goto fun _ => q₁)           (peek' main <|             branch (fun s => natEnd s.iget) (goto fun _ => unrev q₂)               ((push rev fun _ => Γ'.bit0) <| goto fun _ => unrev q₂))   | Λ'.ret (Cont'.cons₁ fs k) =>     goto fun _ =>       move₂ (fun _ => false) main aux <|         move₂ (fun s => s = Γ'.consₗ) stack main <|           move₂ (fun _ => false) aux stack <| trNormal fs (Cont'.cons₂ k)   | Λ'.ret (Cont'.cons₂ k) => goto fun _ => head stack <| Λ'.ret k   | Λ'.ret (Cont'.comp f k) => goto fun _ => trNormal f k   | Λ'.ret (Cont'.fix f k) =>     pop' main <|       goto fun s =>         cond (natEnd s.iget) (Λ'.ret k) <| Λ'.clear natEnd main <| trNormal f (Cont'.fix f k)   | Λ'.ret Cont'.halt => (load fun _ => none) <| halt

      (branch (fun s => decide (s = some Γ'.bit1)) (push rev (fun x => Γ'.bit0) (goto fun x => q.succ))

Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_pred.code:
Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_pred (q₁ q₂ : Λ') :
  tr (q₁.pred q₂) =
    pop' main
      (branch (fun s => decide (s = some Γ'.bit0)) (push rev (fun x => Γ'.bit1) (goto fun x => q₁.pred q₂))
        (branch (fun s => natEnd s.iget) (goto fun x => q₁)
          (peek' main
            (branch (fun s => natEnd s.iget) (goto fun x => unrev q₂)
              (push rev (fun x => Γ'.bit0) (goto fun x => unrev q₂))))))

Turing.PartrecToTM2.trPosNum.comment:
We use `PosNum` to define the translation of binary natural numbers. A natural number is
represented as a little-endian list of `bit0` and `bit1` elements:

    1 = [bit1]
    2 = [bit0, bit1]
    3 = [bit1, bit1]
    4 = [bit0, bit0, bit1]

In particular, this representation guarantees no trailing `bit0`'s at the end of the list.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.trNum.comment:
We use `Num` to define the translation of binary natural numbers. Positive numbers are
translated using `trPosNum`, and `trNum 0 = []`. So there are never any trailing `bit0`'s in
a translated `Num`.

    0 = []
    1 = [bit1]
    2 = [bit0, bit1]
    3 = [bit1, bit1]
    4 = [bit0, bit0, bit1]

Turing.PartrecToTM2.splitAtPred.code: Turing.PartrecToTM2.splitAtPred.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (p : α → Bool) : List α → List α × Option α × List α
Turing.PartrecToTM2.splitAtPred.comment:
This could be a general list definition, but it is also somewhat specialized to this
application. `splitAtPred p L` will search `L` for the first element satisfying `p`.
If it is found, say `L = l₁ ++ a :: l₂` where `a` satisfies `p` but `l₁` does not, then it returns
`(l₁, some a, l₂)`. Otherwise, if there is no such element, it returns `(L, none, [])`.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.fullDefinition: def contSupp : Cont' → Finset Λ'   | Cont'.cons₁ fs k =>     trStmts₁         (move₂ (fun _ => false) main aux <|           move₂ (fun s => s = Γ'.consₗ) stack main <|             move₂ (fun _ => false) aux stack <| trNormal fs (Cont'.cons₂ k)) ∪       (codeSupp' fs (Cont'.cons₂ k) ∪ (trStmts₁ (head stack <| Λ'.ret k) ∪ contSupp k))   | Cont'.cons₂ k => trStmts₁ (head stack <| Λ'.ret k) ∪ contSupp k   | Cont'.comp f k => codeSupp' f k ∪ contSupp k   | Cont'.fix f k => codeSupp' (Code.fix f) k ∪ contSupp k   | Cont'.halt => ∅

Turing.PartrecToTM2.codeSupp.comment:
The (finite!) set of machine states visited during the course of evaluation of `c` in
continuation `k`. This is actually closed under forward simulation (see `tr_supports`), and the
existence of this set means that the machine constructed in this section is in fact a proper
Turing machine, with a finite set of states.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.Supports.comment:
A shorthand for the predicate that we are proving in the main theorems `trStmts₁_supports`,
`codeSupp'_supports`, `contSupp_supports`, `codeSupp_supports`. The set `S` is fixed throughout
the proof, and denotes the full set of states in the machine, while `K` is a subset that we are
currently proving a property about. The predicate asserts that every state in `K` is closed in `S`
under forward simulation, i.e. stepping forward through evaluation starting from any state in `K`
stays entirely within `S`.

          (move₂ (fun s => decide (s = Γ'.consₗ)) stack main

      (codeSupp' fs k.cons₂ ∪ (trStmts₁ (head stack (Λ'.ret k)) ∪ contSupp k))

explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.head: This definition outlines a function that modifies the stack in a Turing machine model by removing a list and pushing its first element onto the main stack.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.splitAtPred.eq_2: This theorem provides an equation for a function that splits a list into parts based on a predicate, indicating how to handle the first element and the remainder of the list recursively.
explanatories.List.Mem.head: This theorem states that the first element of a list is always a member of that list.
explanatories.List.head?: This definition specifies a function that returns the first element of a list, or indicates the absence of an element if the list is empty.
explanatories.Relation.TransGen.head: No information is provided to summarize.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.trList.eq_2: This theorem establishes that the translation of a list that begins with a natural number is equivalent to the translation of that number concatenated with a specific symbol followed by the translation of the rest of the list.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.trStmts₁: This definition describes a set of machine states that can be reached through downward label jumps, excluding those that return to the previous state.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_2.description: This theorem asserts that the support of a continuation constructed by adding an element to the front of another continuation equals the union of the translations of the statements related to the head of a specified stack and the support of the original continuation.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_3.code: Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_3 (f : Code) (k : Cont') : contSupp (Cont'.comp f k) = codeSupp' f k ∪ contSupp k

explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Code.comp: This theorem specifies a particular code in Turing computations that represents the composition operation, allowing the combination of two sequences into a new sequence.
explanatories.Function.comp: Function composition combines two functions into a new function, where the output of the second function becomes the input of the first.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Code.exists_code.comp: This theorem establishes the existence of a specific code in Turing computations that relates the evaluation of two functions, one derived from a vector and the other from finite indices, demonstrating how their compositions yield a unified computational result.
explanatories.Nat.Primrec'.comp: The composition of a primitive recursive function with functions defined for finite input vectors maintains its status as primitive recursive.
explanatories.Nat.Partrec'.comp: The theorem states that if a certain function is partially computable and another set of functions indexed by finite inputs are also partially computable, then a combined function that processes these inputs through a specified mechanism is also partially computable.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.comp: This theorem describes a method for constructing a new continuation in Turing computations by composing a given code with an existing continuation.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.then.eq_3: This theorem illustrates that a specific structure of continuations, when combined with a given list and another continuation, results in a function that modifies the continuation according to the execution of the previous continuation.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.eq_3: This theorem establishes that the normal step operation for Turing computations, when applied to the tail code, results in a new state that retains the continuation and the remainder of the sequence after the first element.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.stepRet.eq_3: This theorem establishes that performing a step in a computational process with a continuation that adds a sequence to the front produces the same result as applying the continuation first and then prepending the head of the sequence to the output.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval.eq_3: This theorem shows that the evaluation of the tail operation in Turing computations produces a result equivalent to directly returning the tail of the input vector.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.eval.eq_3: This theorem establishes that evaluating a continuation constructed with a list of natural numbers and another continuation yields a function that, given any input, results in the evaluation of the second continuation using the first element of the list prepended to that input.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Cont'.comp: This theorem establishes a method for creating a new continuation in a Turing computation by composing a specified code with an existing continuation.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.codeSupp': This definition outlines a finite set of machine states that are encountered during the evaluation of a piece of code, including the state representing the return action but excluding any states following that return.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_3.description: This theorem establishes that the support of a composed continuation is the union of the support of its continuation and the set of states reachable by the code in that continuation.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_4.code: Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_4 (f : Code) (k : Cont') : contSupp (Cont'.fix f k) = codeSupp' f.fix k ∪ contSupp k

explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Code.fix: This theorem defines a specific code in Turing computations that represents a fixed-point operation, allowing the extraction of a function that can be applied repeatedly to itself.
explanatories.PFun.fix: This definition describes a method that transforms a partial function, which may produce either a value or a continuation, into another partial function that returns the first encountered value among those possible, by recursively applying the original function until a definitive value is found or remains undefined.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.fix: This theorem defines a function that takes a specific code and a continuation to produce a new continuation in the context of Turing computations.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.then.eq_4: This theorem establishes an equality relating the composition of a continuation with a function, expressing how the continuation behaves when chained with another continuation.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.stepNormal.eq_4: This theorem establishes an equivalence in Turing computations, showing how the normal stepping of a code that combines two codes can be expressed as a stepping operation on the first code with a specific continuation of the second code.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.stepRet.eq_4: This theorem establishes an equality that relates the result of a continuation step with a composed function to the direct execution of that function with a continuation on a given list.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Code.eval.eq_4: This theorem asserts that evaluating a code consisting of a function followed by a list of functions produces a result that combines the head of the first function's output with the full output of the subsequent functions.
explanatories.Turing.ToPartrec.Cont.eval.eq_4: This theorem demonstrates that the evaluation of a composition of a code with a continuation is equivalent to applying the code's evaluation to the input followed by the evaluation of the continuation.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Cont'.fix: This theorem defines an operation in Turing computations that allows for the creation of a continuation that can repeatedly apply a specified code.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.codeSupp': This definition outlines a finite set of machine states that are encountered during the evaluation of a piece of code, including the state representing the return action but excluding any states following that return.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp.eq_4.description: This theorem demonstrates the equality of the support of a fixed continuation related to a code and a specific continuation with the union of the supports of the code and the original continuation.

explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Λ'.Supports: This definition specifies a condition that requires a state to support certain continuations if the reachable continuations from that state have their support included in a given finite set.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Supports: This definition specifies a property that ensures every state in a given subset remains within a specified set during forward simulation in a Turing machine context.
explanatories.Turing.TM2.Supports: A TM2 machine supports a set of states if every state within that set can only transition to other states also contained in that set.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.contSupp_supports.description: This theorem establishes that if the support of a continuation is contained within a finite set, then that support will also be supported by the finite set itself.

explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Supports: This definition specifies a property that ensures every state in a given subset remains within a specified set during forward simulation in a Turing machine context.
explanatories.Turing.TM2.Supports: A TM2 machine supports a set of states if every state within that set can only transition to other states also contained in that set.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.codeSupp_supports.description: This theorem asserts that if the support of a certain code in Turing computations is contained within a finite set, then it supports that finite set.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_supports.code: Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_supports (c : Code) (k : Cont') : TM2.Supports tr (codeSupp c k)
Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_supports.comment:
The set `codeSupp c k` is a finite set that witnesses the effective finiteness of the `tr`
Turing machine. Starting from the initial state `trNormal c k`, forward simulation uses only
states in `codeSupp c k`, so this is a finite state machine. Even though the underlying type of
state labels `Λ'` is infinite, for a given partial recursive function `c` and continuation `k`,
only finitely many states are accessed, corresponding roughly to subterms of `c`.

explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.codeSupp: This definition specifies a finite set of machine states that are traversed during the evaluation of a given code in a specific continuation, confirming the proper structure of a Turing machine within this context.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Λ'.Supports: This definition specifies a condition that requires a state to support certain continuations if the reachable continuations from that state have their support included in a given finite set.
explanatories.Turing.PartrecToTM2.Supports: This definition specifies a property that ensures every state in a given subset remains within a specified set during forward simulation in a Turing machine context.
explanatories.Turing.TM2.Supports: A TM2 machine supports a set of states if every state within that set can only transition to other states also contained in that set.

Turing.PartrecToTM2.tr_supports.description: This theorem asserts that a specific Turing machine model effectively operates within a finite set of states determined by a given code and continuation, demonstrating its behavior as a finite state machine despite having an infinite set of possible state labels.

ManyOneReducible.code:
ManyOneReducible.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} [Primcodable α] [Primcodable β] (p : α → Prop)
  (q : β → Prop) : Prop
ManyOneReducible.comment:
`p` is many-one reducible to `q` if there is a computable function translating questions about `p`
to questions about `q`.

explanatories.Computable: A function that maps between two types is considered computable if it can be expressed as a partially recursive function when those types are primitively codable.

ManyOneReducible.fullDefinition: def ManyOneReducible {α β} [Primcodable α] [Primcodable β] (p : α → Prop) (q : β → Prop) :=   ∃ f, Computable f ∧ ∀ a, p a ↔ q (f a)
ManyOneReducible.description: A problem is many-one reducible to another if there exists a computable function that allows questions about the first problem to be transformed into questions about the second problem.

AkraBazziRecurrence.GrowsPolynomially.comment:
The growth condition that the function `g` must satisfy for the Akra-Bazzi theorem to apply.
It roughly states that `c₁ g(n) ≤ g(u) ≤ c₂ g(n)`, for `u` between `b*n` and `n` for any
constant `b ∈ (0,1)`.
